readerTitle: How to say no so people still trust your yes
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Apple, 1997년 제품 라인 정리) + 가상 사례 (사내 분석팀, 2인 전기공사 업체)
insight: 좋은 거절은 '아니오'만 말하지 않고, 그 거절이 지키는 '예'와 상대가 대신 할 수 있는 일을 함께 보여준다.
misconception: 거절을 부드럽게 하려면 애매하게 말하거나 답을 미루는 편이 상대에게 더 친절하다.

sources.text: Isaacson, W. (2011). Steve Jobs. Simon & Schuster. (1997년 제품 전략 회의의 2×2 그리드, 제품 라인 축소)
Steve Jobs, Apple Worldwide Developers Conference closing session (1997), 'focus means saying no' 발언
사내 분석팀과 전기공사 업체 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 1997년 Jobs 복귀 당시 Apple이 적자였고 Mac 모델이 지나치게 많았다는 점, 2×2 그리드(Consumer/Pro × Desktop/Portable)를 화이트보드에 그렸다는 점은 Isaacson(2011)을 기준으로 했습니다. 정확한 기존 모델 수는 자료마다 달라 카드에는 'many versions'로만 적었습니다. 게시 전 원문 확인 필요.
'Focus means saying no to many good ideas'는 1997년 WWDC 발언을 풀어 쓴 것(직접 인용 아님)입니다. 카드에서 따옴표 없이 요약으로 썼는지 확인하세요.
Newton 등 일부 제품 단종 시점(1998년)은 카드에 넣지 않았습니다. 추가한다면 별도 확인 필요.

cards.title: How to say no so people still trust your yes
body: In 1997, Steve Jobs returned to an Apple that was losing money and selling many versions of the Mac. Even staff struggled to explain the differences.
He didn't send a long memo. He drew four boxes on a whiteboard. Everything outside those boxes got a no.

image.label: A whiteboard with a simple four-box grid
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 회의실 화이트보드에 2×2 칸 네 개만 그려져 있고, 바닥에는 여러 기기 모형이 상자에 담겨 치워지는 장면. 실제 Apple 로고, 제품 디자인, 인물 얼굴은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: The sales director wants a report by Friday.
body: You lead a three-person analytics team. You've promised the CEO a pricing analysis by the 20th, and it needs everyone.
The sales director asks for a custom weekly report, starting Friday. How do you respond?

options.text: "Let me see what we can do."
options.feedback: It feels polite and avoids conflict now. But the director plans around a maybe, and the real no arrives later, when it hurts more.

options.text: "Not this week. We're on the CEO's pricing work until the 20th. I can show you a filter on the existing dashboard today, or start your report on the 23rd."
options.feedback: Clear, with a reason they can see and two real options. You keep your promise to the CEO and the director can still plan.

options.text: Pass it to your boss and let them decide
options.feedback: You get a clear ruling. But you hand off a call you're best placed to make, and you look less in control of your own priorities.

cards.title: The no came with a picture of the yes.
body: Jobs's grid had two columns, *consumer* and *pro*, and two rows, *desktop* and *portable*. Apple would make one great product in each box. Four in total.

That made every cut easy to understand. Teams didn't hear "your project is bad." They heard "it doesn't fit one of the four boxes." He later described focus as saying no to many good ideas so you can do a few things well.

image.label: Two-by-two grid: consumer and pro, desktop and portable
image.brief: 깔끔한 인포그래픽. 가로 축 "Consumer / Pro", 세로 축 "Desktop / Portable"의 2×2 격자. 각 칸에 단순한 기기 아이콘 하나씩. 격자 밖에 흐리게 처리된 여러 아이콘. 실제 제품 모양이나 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Saying no well
body: **Saying no well** means turning down a request in a way that is clear, honest and useful to the other person. A good no has three parts:
list: **The answer, early:** "No" or "Not this week," not "we'll see"
**The real reason:** the priority it protects, in words they can check
**What they can do instead:** a smaller option, a later date, or someone else who can help
cards.callout: The reason is not an apology. It's the yes you're keeping.

cards.title: A vague no costs more than a clear one.
body: "Maybe" keeps a request alive. The other person waits, plans and follows up. You spend time dodging. When the no finally comes, it lands late and feels like a broken promise.

A clear no ends the uncertainty in one conversation. Because it names a priority, people can disagree with the priority instead of with you. And because it offers a path, they leave with something to do.

cards.title: Customers, bosses and suppliers too.
body: To a customer: "We don't do same-day delivery. We can guarantee tomorrow by 10."
To a boss, a no often works best as a choice: "I can take this on if the launch moves a week. Which matters more?" You're not refusing. You're showing the cost and letting them decide.
cards.softwareNote: Feature requests are the daily version. "That's not on our roadmap because we're focused on faster checkout this quarter. Here's a workaround that gets you most of the way" keeps the user's trust better than "great idea, we'll consider it."

cards.title: Three ways a good no goes wrong.
body: **Over-explaining.** A long list of reasons sounds like an opening bid, and invites people to argue each one.
**Empty alternatives.** Don't offer a later date or a referral you won't follow through on. That's just a slower maybe.
**No to everything.** If you're turning down most requests, the problem may be your priorities, not your wording. A clear no only works when the yes behind it is worth protecting.

cards.title: Now it's a two-person electrical firm.
body: You're booked solid for six weeks. A loyal past customer calls: could you rewire their kitchen next week before their new appliances arrive?

options.text: "I'll call you if something opens up."
options.feedback: It sounds kind and keeps the door open. But they may stop looking for anyone else, and miss their deadline waiting for a call that never comes.

options.text: "I can't next week. We're booked until mid-month. I can hold the 15th for you, or give you the number of an electrician I trust who may be free."
options.feedback: They get a firm answer today and two real paths. You protect your current clients and stay the person they call first next time.

options.text: Quote a very high price and let them decide
options.feedback: Fine if you'd truly take the job at that price. As a hidden no, it can feel like gouging to someone who trusted you.

cards.softwareNote: The same pattern helps any small service team, including a software agency fielding a rush project from a past client.

cards.title: Say no early, say why, and show the way forward.
body: A good no protects what you've already promised and still leaves the other person better off than a maybe would.
**Try it today:** find one request you've been answering with "let me see." Reply with a clear answer, the priority behind it, and one thing they can do instead.
